title: palmy API
description: Every exported procedure and type in the palmy package, with its doc comment, grouped by file. Read from palmy/*.odin.
hast: Every exported procedure and type in the
package: 277 procedures and 72 types across 24 files. Each entry is the declaration as written and the comment above it in the source; declarations marked
are left out. The guides under
explain how the pieces fit together.
Config describes the window to open. Everything has a usable default, so
is a complete program's worth of setup.

create connects to the compositor, opens a window and gets it configured.
The returned App is heap allocated so that the context pointers handed to
your frame body stay valid.
quit_app asks the frame loop to stop after the current frame.
redraw forces another frame even if nothing changed.

It is only valid from the frame loop's own thread, because it is a plain
write to the frame state. A worker thread wants
wake asks for one more frame. Safe from any thread; see
wake_after arms a one-shot that runs one frame after

and then
disarms itself. Arming is earliest-wins; see
wake_at arms the one-shot for an instant rather than a delay.

frames_presented is how many frames this window has actually put on screen.
An idle palmy window's count does not move, which is what makes "did that
wake cost exactly one frame?" a question a test can ask.

Each iteration is one presented frame. The call blocks while the window is
idle, so a palmy app uses no CPU when nothing is happening.

direct_frames is the no-UI loop: it hands you the window's pixel buffer each
vsync and presents whatever you wrote.

key_repeat_timeout is how long an app that blocks on descriptors of its
own between frames may sleep before a held key's next repeat is due, in
milliseconds; -1 when no key is held. Such an app must wake by then, or
held keys repeat only as often as something else wakes it.

key_pressed reports whether a keysym was pressed this frame. Use the KEY_*
constants, or a character literal for printable keys.

decides whether auto-repeat counts. Leave it on for a
movement key, where holding the key should keep moving; turn it off for a
command, where one press must mean one action — a held Backspace that walks
a file browser up three directories is this distinction going wrong.

This answers "was it pressed", not "how many times". Several presses can
land in one frame, and they collapse to a single

move one row, and synthetic input hits this immediately because a driver
script sends keys far faster than a human. When one press must equal one
step — navigation, a nudge, stepping a value — count with

key_count is how many times a key arrived this frame. Several presses can
land in one frame, and a boolean cannot tell one from three.
shortcut matches a key with modifiers, e.g.

.
Auto-repeat is excluded by default: a shortcut is a command, and holding it
down should not fire it repeatedly.
wheel is the wheel movement this frame in notches rather than raw units.

set_focus moves keyboard focus to an element, so an app that manages its own
panes can take focus back from a widget that grabbed it.
focus_id is whatever currently holds keyboard focus.

typed_text returns the characters produced this frame, after the keymap has
had its say. Valid until the end of the frame.
Order matters in a form: take the text

acting on keys. A password
and the Return that submits it can arrive in the same frame, and handling
Return first submits a truncated value.
mouse_pos is the pointer position in logical pixels.
size is the window's logical size.
delta_time is the seconds elapsed since the previous frame.
elapsed is the seconds since the first frame, handy for animations.
frames_per_second is a smoothed frame rate, for debug overlays.

window_scale is the device pixels per logical pixel of the output the window
is on, which palmy follows automatically.
app_elapsed is the seconds since the first frame.
app_delta is the seconds the previous frame took.
pointer is the pointer position in logical pixels.
pointer_down reports a held mouse button.
pressed_key reports a keysym pressed since the previous frame.

host_keymap is the XKB keymap this process was given by the compositor.
A nested compositor forwards it to its own clients.
describe returns a one-line summary of the backend, for diagnostics.

Bidi_Class is the Bidi_Class property: the 23 values UAX #9 reasons about.
The order matters only in that the generated table at the foot of this file
names these variants, so changing the order means regenerating it.
Bidi_Direction is the base direction a caller asks for.

runs P2/P3 —
the direction comes from the first strong character, which is what a text
field holding user-supplied text wants.

force it, which is what
a UI with a known locale wants: an empty RTL search box should still put its
caret on the right.

Bidi_Run is one maximal stretch of text at a single embedding level, as a
half-open byte range into the string that was resolved.

in order, left to right, advancing the pen
by each run's width. Within a run of odd level the

still run
right to left, so the run's own codepoints are drawn from

Bidi_Layout is the answer: the runs in visual order plus the per-character
levels a caret needs.

position in logical order, which
is the order the string is stored in.

has one extra entry holding
the string length, so
bidi_is_rtl reports whether an embedding level runs right to left.

bidi_layout_rtl reports whether the paragraph as a whole is right-to-left,
which is what decides where an empty line's caret sits and which edge

Bidi_Scratch holds every buffer the algorithm needs. It is reusable and
reused:

clears it and refills it, so after the first few
calls it stops allocating entirely. One per text-laying-out thing — a
, a text widget, a frame — is the intended shape.
bidi_scratch_init gives the scratch its allocator. Calling it is optional:

on
first use. Call it explicitly to put the buffers in an arena instead.

bidi_scratch_destroy releases the buffers. A scratch living in an arena that
is freed wholesale does not need this.

bidi_class returns a codepoint's Bidi_Class. Unassigned codepoints get the
DerivedBidiClass default for their block, so an as-yet-unassigned Arabic
codepoint behaves as AL rather than drifting left-to-right.
bidi_mirror returns the glyph to draw in place of

inside a right-to-left
run — rule L4. An opening parenthesis in Hebrew text is still an opening
parenthesis, so it must be drawn as

, pointing into the text rather than
away from it. Characters with no mirror come back unchanged, so a caller can
apply this unconditionally.
has a mirrored form at all.

bidi_is_control reports whether a codepoint is one of the invisible
directional controls, or any other boundary-neutral character. These carry
levels — they have to, or runs would fragment around them — but they have no
width and no glyph, and a caller must not try to draw them.

bidi_bracket looks up the Bidi_Paired_Bracket property — the data rule BD16
pairs brackets with.

is
the other half of the pair. Beyond BD16 this is what an editor needs to
highlight a matching bracket, so it is public.

bidi_base_level resolves just the paragraph level, for a caller that needs
to know which edge is the start — where to park a caret in an empty field,
or which way to align — without resolving the whole string.

bidi_resolve runs the whole algorithm over one paragraph and returns the
runs in visual order together with the per-character levels.

, and the next call with the same scratch
overwrites them.
bidi_rune_index maps a byte offset to the rune position

is indexed
by. An offset inside a multi-byte character resolves to that character.

bidi_level_at is the embedding level of the character containing a byte
offset, or the paragraph level for an empty string. A caret uses it to decide
which way typing will grow the text and which direction an arrow key moves.

bidi_visual_order writes the logical rune indices in visual order, left to
right, into a caller-provided buffer and returns how many it wrote — which
is the rune count, so

is enough, and is cheaper. A
per-character map is for the things that genuinely are per-character — hit
testing inside a run, drawing a selection rectangle, or stepping a caret
visually rather than logically.

bidi_direction_for_level turns a resolved base level back into the forced
direction that reproduces it.

This is how a wrapped paragraph gives each of its lines the paragraph's own
direction. L1 resets trailing whitespace and L2 reorders per

, so every
line has to be resolved separately — but resolving each one

lets a
line that happens to begin with a Latin word flip to left-to-right in the
middle of a Hebrew paragraph. Resolve

once over the whole
paragraph, pass it through here, and hand the result to every line.

bidi_class_needs_resolve reports whether a class can make a left-to-right
paragraph reorder: a strong right-to-left type, an Arabic number, or one of
the explicit embedding, override and isolate controls.

Everything else — L, EN, the separators, the neutrals, NSM, BN — resolves to
an even level under an even base level, and L2 reverses nothing when no odd
level is present. (EN does rise two levels under I1, which is why the test is
about oddness rather than about the level being zero.)

bidi_cannot_reorder reports that a string's visual order is certainly its
logical order under a left-to-right base direction, so the caller may skip
entirely and walk the codepoints as it always has.

This is the cheap test the module header promises. The common case — every
byte below 0x80 — costs one pass of byte comparisons, because no ASCII
character is R, AL, AN or an explicit control. Above that, only codepoints
from U+0590 up can be any of those (Hebrew is the first right-to-left block,
and LRM/RLM, ALM and the isolates all sit higher), so Latin-1, Latin
Extended, Greek, Cyrillic and every CJK string are decided by the range test
alone and never reach the class table.

A true answer is a promise; a false answer is only a suspicion, and the
caller resolves to find out.

Rect is an axis-aligned rectangle. Positions are in pixels and may be
fractional; everything antialiases against the pixel grid.

and returns the rectangles that are
left: the band above, the band below, and the two beside. A clip is one
rectangle with no exclusion, so this is how to clip to everything

itself, and a hole that covers
it gives back nothing. For the specific case of a shadow around an opaque
box,

does the same thing in one call and without the
clip stack.

Paint describes how a shape is filled: either a flat color or a two-stop
linear gradient along one axis.

Canvas is a 32-bit XRGB pixel buffer plus a clip stack. The pixel memory is
usually the compositor's shared-memory buffer, so writes land straight in the
window with no intermediate copy.
push_clip intersects the clip region and remembers the previous one.
put writes one pixel, ignoring alpha.
get reads one pixel back as a color.
blend composites one pixel with src-over alpha blending.
fill_rect fills an axis-aligned rectangle, antialiasing fractional edges.
clamp_radius keeps radii from overlapping on small boxes, the way CSS does.

fill_round_rect_paint fills a rounded rectangle. Rows that cross a corner are
evaluated through a signed distance field for clean antialiasing; the rows in
between are filled as flat spans, which keeps large panels cheap.
stroke_round_rect draws a border inside the given rectangle.

drop_shadow draws a soft shadow for a rounded rectangle. The falloff is a
smoothstep over the shape's distance field, which is a good approximation of
a gaussian blur and costs a fraction as much.

with a rectangle the caller promises
to paint over opaquely, which is nearly always the shape casting the shadow.
Nothing inside it is drawn at all, so the cost is the soft ring rather than
the whole interior.

Pass it only when the cover really is opaque: under a translucent panel the
shadow is visible through it, and skipping it there would show as a bright
rectangle.

draws every pixel, which is
always safe. Partly-covered edge pixels are still drawn, so a fractional
rectangle does not leave a seam.

measured an A4 page's shadow at 11.7 ms a frame and cut it to 3.6 ms
by clipping

into four bands around the page; this is that, in
one call. See
draw_line draws an antialiased line of the given thickness.

srgb_to_linear converts one sRGB channel byte to linear light, 0..1. An
application compositing its own coverage -- a glyph cache, a blur, anything
that blends partial alpha -- wants this pair rather than blending the bytes
directly, which darkens light-on-dark and thickens dark-on-light.
Both are table-driven and exact to the byte:

returns the
same value the reference

linear_to_srgb converts linear light, 0..1, back to an sRGB channel byte.
See
blend_coverage composites one pixel of antialiased coverage in linear light.
blit_mask composites an 8-bit coverage mask, which is how glyphs are drawn.

Cursor names the pointer shape an element asks for. They map onto
cursor-shape-v1, so the compositor draws its own themed cursor.

Style is the fully resolved appearance and layout of one node. Anything the
class parser can express lives here, and the fields marked "inherited" flow
down to children the way they do in CSS.

Interaction is the state a node was in when it was last on screen. The class
parser uses it to decide whether

style_default is the root style: the CSS initial values, adjusted to
Tailwind's preflight (no margins, border-box sizing everywhere).

apply_classes walks a Tailwind-style class list and folds each utility into
the style. Variant prefixes (

Clip_Kind is which of the two selections: the clipboard proper (Ctrl+C,
Ctrl+V) or the primary selection (select, middle-click).

clipboard_set puts text on the clipboard. It returns false when there is no
window, the display server has no clipboard protocol, it refused, or this is
not the frame loop's thread.
clipboard_get reads the clipboard as UTF-8 text.

is false when there
is nothing on it that is text, or it could not be read; an empty clipboard
is ("", false).
primary_set makes text the primary selection, what a middle click pastes.

clipboard_available reports whether this window can reach a clipboard
natively: Wayland with wl_data_device_manager, or any X11 server.
A color in non-premultiplied sRGB with 8 bits per channel.
is_current reports whether a colour is the

current_over resolves the stand-in against the text colour it stands for,
keeping whatever opacity the token asked for.
hex takes 0xRRGGBB and returns an opaque color.

hexa takes 0xRRGGBBAA -- alpha is the LOW byte, not the high one. A canvas
word is 0xAARRGGBB, so the two orders differ and reading one as the other is
silent: 0x08ffffff meant as 3% white comes back as opaque cyan.
fade scales a color's alpha by
mix linearly interpolates between two colors, including their alpha.

luminance is the perceptual brightness of a color, 0..1. Handy for deciding
whether text on top of it should be light or dark.
parse_color resolves a Tailwind-style color token.
suffix sets the alpha as a percentage, matching Tailwind's opacity modifier.
Damage_Rect is a changed region in buffer pixels.

Damage_State, frame_damage and damage_destroy are public only so the tests
can drive them; a window keeps its own.

(bw x bh) with the last frame sent and
fills d.rects with what changed; it returns false when nothing did. The
shadow copy is brought up to date as a side effect, so it must be called
only for a frame that is then actually sent (or skipped because it is
identical).
load_emoji_font pins the colour-bitmap emoji font, overriding discovery.
emoji_font_path reports which file backs colour emoji, or "" for none.

emoji_strike_ppem reports the pixel size of the strike in use, for
diagnostics and tests. Zero means no emoji font was found.

Font_Weight covers the four weights real interfaces use. shadcn leans on
medium and semibold constantly, and collapsing them onto regular/bold is
visible immediately in a side-by-side.

Font_Slant is the second axis of a face, and it is not a weight. Emphasis in
running text — markdown

, a Quote block, an italic spreadsheet
cell — is a slant; rendering it as semibold upright is the wrong glyphs, and
parking a real italic file in an unused

slot is a workaround
for a missing axis rather than a design.

Fonts owns the loaded faces and a cache of rasterized glyphs, keyed by
family, weight, slant, integer pixel size and codepoint.
Metrics describes a font at one size, in pixels.

load_font pins one font file to a family, weight and slant, overriding
discovery. The parity renderer uses it to load exactly the files the browser
loads.

A path that does not exist is looked up again by file name under the system
font directories. Applications pin fonts by the absolute path they have on a
development machine -- the kit loads Geist out of the parity tree -- and on
an installed system the same file lives in /usr/share/fonts instead. Without
this second look every such application silently drops to whatever the scan
picked, which on a minimal system means a different typeface per window.

use_synthetic_italic replaces a family/weight's italic slot with a sheared
copy of its own upright face, discarding whatever real italic discovery
found. An application that swaps its primaries for a family shipping no
italic wants exactly this: a sheared Geist still reads as Geist, where a real
Noto Sans Italic set beside Geist reads as a bug.

font_is_synthetic reports whether a slot is being faked rather than loaded:
a bold overprinted from a lighter face, or an italic sheared from upright.

load_fallback_font appends a face to the fallback chain. An application only
needs this for a script the automatic scan did not find a font for; the
chain is searched in the order faces are added.
font_path reports which file backs a family, weight and slant.
font_metrics returns the ascent, descent and natural line height in pixels.
text_width measures a single line of text in pixels.

is the base direction the line inherits from its paragraph, and only
matters for text that reorders; see the bidirectional section below. The
width of a reordered line is not the width of the same characters laid out in
storage order — shaping changes which glyphs are drawn, and kerning applies
to a different set of pairs — so this cannot be answered without doing the
reordering, and it is done by the same procedure the drawing uses.
draw_text draws one line with its baseline at

draw_text_outlined draws a line with a stroke around every glyph, which is
what a subtitle needs to stay legible over any frame behind it.
The stroke is the glyph's own coverage mask dilated by

, computed once
per (glyph, size, width) and cached. Drawing the run eight times at offsets
costs eight rasterisations and still leaves an octagonal halo at the joins;
this costs one, and the join is round.

text_index_at maps a pixel offset back to a byte index in the string — which
is what every text cursor needs: clicking into a paragraph, dragging a
selection, or deciding where a caret lands after a vertical move.
The returned index is always on a rune boundary, and is the

rather than the one before it, so clicking the right half of
a character puts the caret after it.

text_width_upto measures the string up to a byte index, which is where a
caret at that index sits. Pair it with

For text laid out left to right that is the whole story and this is still
literally the width of the prefix, which is what the forty-odd callers of it
mean. For text that reorders it is not:

can contain characters
drawn to the right of the caret, so the prefix has no edge to measure and the
question has to be asked of the visual runs instead. Such a string is handed
to

, which is the honest form of this procedure and takes the
affinity a direction boundary needs.
Caret_Affinity resolves the one thing a byte offset cannot say on its own.
At a direction boundary a single logical index has

is both
the right edge of

— the same character offset,
two places, and no amount of further measurement decides between them,
because the information is not in the string. It comes from how the caret got
there: typing after
means one, clicking to the right of
So the affinity travels beside the index:
Downstream  the caret precedes the character

, and is drawn at
that character's leading edge — its left side in a
left-to-right run, its right side in a right-to-left one.
Upstream    the caret follows the character

, and is drawn
at that character's trailing edge.

For text with one direction the two agree everywhere, which is why every
entry point defaults to

and why nothing already written needs to
care.

Text_Glyph is one glyph of a laid-out line: what to draw, where, and which
bytes of the original string it stands for.
The list is in visual order, left to right.

includes the kern applied in front of the glyph — so hit
testing is a search for the box containing a coordinate, and

is the
offset from the box to where the glyph is actually painted.

are the inverse of the whole transformation, and the only
way back. A lam-alef ligature has

spanning two letters, which is why a
byte offset cannot be recovered from the drawn codepoint alone.

Text_Span is one rectangle's horizontal extent, relative to the line origin.
A selection is a list of these rather than a single pair of edges, because a
logical range that crosses a direction boundary is discontiguous on screen.

Caret_Step is a direction on screen, not in the string. Arrow keys are the
one place a text field has to choose: logical movement steps the byte offset,
visual movement steps left and right as the reader sees them, and inside a
right-to-left run those are opposites. Most toolkits use visual for the arrow
keys and logical for word jumps;

text_base_dir resolves a paragraph's base direction to the forced direction
its lines should each be resolved with. Pass the whole paragraph, use the
answer for every line of it.

text_base_rtl reports whether a line's own base direction is right to left,
which is what decides where

alignment puts it and where an empty
field parks its caret.

is 1 for that
reason: an empty right-to-left search box still wants its caret on the right.

text_caret_x is where the caret sits for a logical byte offset, measured from
the line origin.

wanted to be and could not: once a
line reorders, the caret's x stops being a function of the prefix of the
string, because
contains characters that are drawn to the

of the caret. The answer is an edge of a glyph in the visual list,
and which edge is what

with the answer it had to throw
away: which side of the character the hit landed on, and therefore which of
the two visual positions a boundary offset means.
Inside a right-to-left run the logical index

as x increases, so
the midpoint test flips: a hit on the right half of a right-to-left character
is a caret before it, not after it.

with the rectangles that highlight the
logical byte range
, and returns how many it wrote.

A selection stops being one rectangle the moment a range crosses a direction
boundary: the characters are contiguous in the string and in two places on
screen. Visually adjacent runs of selected glyphs are merged, so selecting a
whole mixed line is still one rectangle, and selecting across its boundary is
two. Two spans is enough for one boundary; a line alternating direction
several times needs more, and a caller that passes a short buffer gets the
leftmost spans and a count equal to its length.
text_caret_move steps the caret one character to the left or the right

, which in a right-to-left run is the opposite of stepping the byte
offset.

The caret is identified by the glyph it is attached to and the side of it,
which is what the index and affinity together say. Moving crosses exactly one
glyph, and the caret arrives on its far side — stated in terms of that
glyph's own direction, so the returned affinity is the one that puts the
caret back where this procedure left it. At either end of the line the caret
does not move and the input comes back unchanged, which is the signal to try
the next line.

text_glyphs lays out a line and hands back the glyph list, for the callers
that genuinely need it: an editor drawing per-character decoration, a
truncation that has to happen visually rather than on the logical prefix, or
a test reading back what was drawn.

and the next text call overwrites it. Copy
it or finish with it.
draw_icon stamps an icon at the given top-left corner.

rotates it
about its centre, measured in whole turns, so a spinner is just the frame
clock:
load_image decodes a file from disk.

image_size reads the dimensions without decoding the pixels, which is what a
file browser wants for a listing.
image_destroy frees the pixels. A view from

borrows another
image's buffer, so destroying one is a no-op rather than a double free.
is_image_path is a cheap extension check, for deciding whether to try.
image_rotated returns a view of the whole image, turned clockwise by
(negative turns anticlockwise). A quarter turn swaps
, so layout and object-fit see the turned shape.

image_window returns a view of one rectangle of the image, turned clockwise
by

image's pixels, which
is what panning a rotated picture means:

are how far into the
picture the window starts as you see it, not as it is stored.

A window that runs off the edge is clamped to the image, so a pan can be
driven straight from a scroll offset without the caller checking bounds.
Fit decides how an image fills the box it is given, matching CSS object-fit.
fitted_rect computes where an image lands inside a box under a fit mode.

draw_image scales an image into a destination rectangle. Sampling is
bilinear when scaling down or up smoothly, and nearest when magnified past
2x so that a zoomed-in photo shows its actual pixels rather than mush.

write_png_rgba saves raw RGBA bytes as a PNG. Handy for screenshots, and for
any app that needs to export what it drew.

Custom_Fn is the escape hatch: a procedure handed the node's rectangle and
the raw canvas, free to write whatever pixels it likes.
Ctx is the per-frame UI context. It is handed to you by

and is the
single argument every element takes.

key names the next element explicitly. Use it for list items so that their
state follows the item rather than the slot it happens to occupy.

state returns a pointer to a value that persists across frames, created the
first time it is asked for. This is palmy's useState:
div opens a container. Close it with
end closes the container opened by the matching

with the direction already set, since that is how most
containers start out.

group builds a subtree with a callback, which keeps nesting visible without
a matching
. The user pointer is passed straight through.

text adds a run of text. It wraps to the width it is given unless the class
list says

with formatting. The formatted string lives in the frame
arena, so there is nothing to free.
divider draws a hairline across the cross axis.

pixels hands you the canvas for a rectangle of the layout. Everything in
canvas.odin is available, as is writing to

is borrowed until the frame is painted, which happens after the whole
frame has been built -- not at this call. So it must outlive the frame, and
two things that look fine are dangling by then: a struct on the stack of the

that something

the class (

) and otherwise follows the font size, the way an inline
SVG does in a browser.

and
magnifies around the centre for a viewer that can zoom in.

To turn it, or to show one part of it, hand it a view instead of the image.
A view borrows the same pixels and costs nothing to make, and

report
what it presents, so layout and object-fit see the turned or cropped shape:

clone_frame copies a string into the frame arena, which is reset at the top
of every frame. It is what

does with what it is handed, and it is the
answer whenever a string has to outlive the statement that built it but not
the frame -- a number formatted for a label, a path shortened for a title.

is the same arena for the common case of joining pieces; this is
the one-argument version for a string that already exists. Do not keep what
it returns past

rect_of returns where a node was drawn last frame, which is what hit testing
and scrolling work from.
hovered reports whether the pointer is over the node with this id.

node_rect returns where an element was laid out, in logical pixels. It is
valid once the frame has been finished, and from the next frame onwards it is
also what hit testing uses.
node_id is an element's stable identity, for use with

node_count is the number of elements built so far this frame, which is also
the index the next element will take. Pair it with

to find out
where a widget ended up:

style returns the resolved style of the element that was created last, so it
can be adjusted directly when a class string will not do:
The pointer is only valid until the next element is created.

node_parent, node_kind and node_text expose the built tree, which is what
the parity renderer dumps alongside its pixels so geometry can be compared
numerically rather than only visually.

widget_caret exposes a text field's caret: the byte offset it sits at and
which side of that offset it is on. The affinity is not redundant -- at a
direction boundary one offset has two screen positions, so a test that only
read the offset could not tell a correct caret from a wrong one.

widget_cursor is widget_caret's offset alone, for callers that do not care
which edge the caret is drawn on.

node_lines exposes the wrapped lines of a text node: the string each line
holds, the width it measured, and the base direction it was resolved with.
The direction is the interesting one -- it is per paragraph, not per line,
and a test asserting that a wrapped right-to-left paragraph did not change
direction partway down needs to see it.

apply folds more utilities into the element created last. It is how variant
systems compose: a base class string, then the variant, then the size, each
overriding what came before, exactly like

concat joins strings into the frame arena. Class strings often have to be
assembled at runtime — a variant name, a side suffix, a size — and this keeps
that allocation-free from the caller's point of view, since the arena is
reset every frame.
scroll_of reads a scroll container's current offset.
scroll_extent is how far a container can scroll on each axis.
scroll_to sets a container's offset, clamped to what it can actually scroll.
scroll_nudge moves a container by a delta. (

is the offscreen
renderer's synthetic wheel input, which is a different thing.)

wake_window asks the frame loop to run one more frame.

It is safe to call from any thread. It takes no lock, allocates nothing and
never blocks — an atomic store and a write to an eventfd — so calling it
while the loop is in the middle of drawing, from inside the loop itself, or
from a signal handler, cannot deadlock.

One call means at most one extra frame. The loop drains the descriptor, runs
a single iteration and parks again; it does not start spinning.
wake_after_window arms a one-shot: the loop sleeps at most

and then
runs a frame. It fires once and disarms itself — nothing repeats until it is
armed again.

Arming is earliest-wins. Two subsystems each asking for a wake both get
served by the nearer deadline, and an already-armed nearer deadline is not
pushed out by a later request. The natural way to use it is to re-arm every
frame with whatever the next thing to happen is; the natural way to misuse
it is to arm once for a far-off instant and expect a nearer, unrelated wake
not to consume it.
A delay of zero or less is the same as
wake_at_window arms the one-shot for an instant rather than a delay.

wake_cancel_window disarms the one-shot. A wake already turned into a
pending frame is not taken back.
